extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of history/literary criticism; students studying heroic characterization
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and qualities for depicting or evaluating 'great men' (heroes, prophets, national leaders) in biographical or critical prose; emphasizes moral, rhetorical, and practical traits illustrated by Luther and Knox. Useful for writers crafting heroic character-portraits or critics assessing greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idol-breaker / Prophet who returns men to reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic function is to be a 'Prophet Idol-breaker' — a bringer-back of men to reality; to tell men that God's-world stands not on semblances but on realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Luther burning the Pope's Bull as denouncing 'semblances' (indulgences, Popeship) and insisting on God's truth. Anti-pattern: celebrating forms and 'Simulacra' that keep people in comfortable falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity (primary characteristic of a hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero is fundamentally sincere — he holds to the truth and fact; the truth alone is there for him, the rest mere shadow and deceptive nonentity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Knox's refusal to worship an image in the galleys ('a pented bredd'). Scoring note: sincerity includes consistency of conviction even when unpopular or costly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience-driven integrity / refusal to recant without proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts according to conscience and will not do 'aught against conscience'; will recant only if confuted by Scripture or plain just arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Luther at the Diet of Worms: 'Here stand I; I can do no other.' Anti-pattern: capitulation to power for safety or favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage and valor, not mere ferocity
rubrics_metrics.description: True courage is fearless confrontation of spiritual or moral enemies, combined with gentleness and pity — not coarse ferocity or savage obstinacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Luther's defiance of 'Devils' and physical threats but also his tenderness and affection. Anti-pattern: tiger-like fury that lacks thought or compassion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discernment between essential and non-essential (measured tolerance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine tolerance consists in distinguishing what is essential from what is not; the unessential may be allowed, the essential must be defended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Luther allowing a preacher to wear a cassock if it helps him preach. Practical advice: tolerate harmless forms; be firm on core truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership stability / ability to hold a movement peaceably
rubrics_metrics.description: A great leader can remain the 'sovereign' centre of a revolution, keeping the movement from degenerating into violence and confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Luther continuing to guide Protestants so disputes did not immediately become fighting while he lived. Scoring note: measure by capacity to rally others and maintain order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical and literary force
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero's words and writings are potent instruments of change ('His words are half-battles'); strong idiomatic expression can cleave to the secret of the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Luther's robust, idiomatic writings and memorable phrases. Anti-pattern: dull, abstract prose that fails to mobilize feeling or action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical wisdom and sound judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A leader must discern 'where the true heart of the matter lies' and plant himself courageously there; give wise courses that others can follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Luther's moderation in controversies (Karlstadt, Anabaptists, Peasants' War). Measure: ability to select practical policies and sustain them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility and non-self-seeking greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: True greatness is simple, spontaneous, not self-proclaimed; a hero is 'for quite another purpose than being great.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Carlyle's image of an Alpine mountain — immense yet unassuming. Anti-pattern: ostentatious ambition and performative grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation and transfusion of the good in the Old
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not prematurely destroy old institutions; the 'Old' remains until its soul of good has been transfused into the practical New.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: retain what can still do good; only reject forms once their beneficial substance has been appropriated into new practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral seriousness, earnestness, and capacity for sorrow
rubrics_metrics.description: The basis of a great life is Sadness and Earnestness — deep feeling, resignation, longing for rest, and a heartfelt seriousness about human destiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Luther's melancholy, tears, and weary longing in later life. Creative note: include pathos and interior depth when portraying heroes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to speak truth to power / rebuke authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero will confront rulers and institutions when truth demands it, even at the cost of personal peril or unpopularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Knox's harsh visits and reprovals to Queen Mary. Anti-pattern: courtierly politeness that sacrifices the nation's or cause's truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of a believing nation / nation-forming moral leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic leadership may act as the seed of a national spirit (a 'nation of heroes') by bringing a people into a sincere, heart-based faith and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Puritanism/Knox catalyzing Scotland and New England; the Mayflower settlers forming America's soul. Measure: long-term cultural and institutional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured intolerance when necessary (active resistance to Falsehood)
rubrics_metrics.description: While tolerant of unessentials, the hero does not tolerate falsehoods and iniquities that fasten on the people — he resists and seeks to extinguish them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: this intolerance is principled and directed at core falsehoods, not at mere difference of harmless practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reluctant or emergent leadership (not self-appointed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Often the prophetic post comes not from seeking but from circumstance; a hero may be thrust into leadership and initially resist or feel inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Knox breaking into tears when first called to speak. Characterization tip: portray initial reluctance to heighten authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to suffer personal cost for the cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroism commonly involves exile, imprisonment, physical hardship, or social ostracism endured for the truth or nation's welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Knox rowed in galleys and wandered in exile; Luther faced threats and estrangement. Scoring: willingness to accept sacrifice is central.
